title: Sukhmani whole

cards: There's a difference between studying a mosaic tile by tile and stepping back to see the picture. Up close, each tile is a small square of color: blue, gold, a chip of red.
Step back across the room, and suddenly there's a face, a tree, a whole scene. The tiles didn't change. You just saw them together.
We've looked at Sukhmani tile by tile since day four hundred thirty-six. Today, the whole picture.

teach.b: Sukhmani Sahib was written by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who also compiled the Adi Granth, the scripture that became the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition places its writing at Ramsar, a pool in Amritsar.
It sits in raag Gauri, and it's long: twenty-four ashtpadis.
Ashtpadi means eight steps; each has a salok and then eight stanzas. Seen whole, it has a shape. It opens with remembering: simrau simar simar sukh paavau, remembering, I find peace.
Early on it praises simran and the company of the holy, and names the qualities of the God-conscious person.
In the middle it turns honest about us: pride, slander, cleverness, leaning on mortals, wealth that stays behind. Then it lifts toward refuge: the wanderer at the door, the beggar asking for mercy.
Toward the end it opens out to the largest things: the stillness before creation, the Lord of all beings, the cleared eyes that see God within and without.
And it closes on the perfect One and the peace of the Name, back where it began.
Not a list: a journey, from remembering, through an honest look at ourselves, to refuge, to wonder, to peace.
Some Sikhs recite it in one sitting, daily or weekly, and families and sangats gather in homes and gurdwaras to recite it together, in hard times or at a family's milestones.
Read whole, it takes time. That's part of the gift: a long stretch where nothing is asked of you but to listen.

how: Sikhs recite Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's twenty-four ashtpadis in raag Gauri, in a single sitting, daily or weekly, and groups gather in homes and gurdwaras to recite it together.

games.q: you step back from Sukhmani like a mosaic. what shape does the whole make?
o: a journey: remembering, honesty, refuge, wonder, peace.
a single story about one person.
games.why: from simran at the start, through an honest look at ourselves, to refuge, the wonder of creation, and the peace of the Name.

practice: Sit quietly and let the shape of the journey pass slowly through your mind, remembering, honesty, refuge, wonder, peace, one tile at a time until you see the picture.
Sukhmani can be heard whole in Gurmukhi, in translation or on a recording whenever you have a long, quiet stretch; for now, just rest with its shape. If you pray, rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Sukhmani whole. Guru Arjan's twenty-four ashtpadis, read in one sitting, make a journey from remembering, through honesty and refuge, to wonder and peace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sukhmani, often rendered jewel of peace, or peace of mind.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole jewel. Tile by tile, and now the picture. Day five hundred thirty-four, done.
